pseudo_labeling.summary: A network learns from the labelled bars and from its own hard predictions on unlabelled bars, weighted in slowly (Lee 2013).
pseudo_labeling.implementationNote: Bridge: P(up) is the sigmoid of one network trained on labelled bars plus its own hard predictions on unlabelled bars, weighted in linearly. Differs from the spec: Labels are masked in embargoed blocks so there is an unlabelled pool. That deliberately handicaps the model against full supervision. No price model (a regressor pseudo-labelling itself gets no gradient). Expect: near the plain network; on weak labels it confirms its own mistakes.

ramp_epochs.description: Epochs from the ramp start to the full weight (T2 - T1).

native.produces: A probability for each class of a bar from one network that was trained on the labelled bars and on its own hard guesses for the unlabelled bars.
native.targetVariable: the class label of an input row, which here is whether the close a fixed number of bars ahead is above the current bar's close
native.objectiveNote: Lee's version adds to the cross-entropy on labelled bars a second cross-entropy against the network's own hard prediction on unlabelled bars, with a weight that starts at zero and is ramped up so that early wrong guesses carry little force, while the specification describes the thresholded form that admits only confident guesses into a growing labelled set.

metrics.why: The network is trained by cross-entropy on true labels and then on its own guesses, so the honest test of what came out is how much probability it gave to what really happened on bars it never trained on.
metrics.baseline: the logarithmic loss of quoting the fold's training up share on every scored bar

metrics.why: Pseudo-labeling claims that feeding the network its own guesses improves it, and the only direct test is the score of the identical network with the pseudo-label weight held at zero, on identical folds.
metrics.baseline: the same network trained with the pseudo-label weight at zero on the same labelled bars

metrics.why: A network that is rewarded for agreeing with its own hard guess is pulled toward stating more extreme odds on the unlabelled bars, and a slope below one shows that this confirmation loop made it over-confident.
metrics.baseline: a slope of one, which means the stated odds have the right scale

metrics.why: A bounded score of the network's probability that a handful of very confident self-taught misses cannot dominate, read beside the logarithmic loss for that reason.
metrics.baseline: the Brier score of quoting the fold's training up share on every scored bar

metrics.why: Even when the self-confirming loss distorts the size of the odds, the network's logit may still order up bars above down bars, and this number measures that ordering alone.
metrics.baseline: one half, the value of an ordering that carries no information

metrics.why: The method rests on the assumption that the network's most confident guesses are its most correct ones, so the up share inside its highest-confidence bin against the up share of all scored bars tests that assumption directly.
metrics.baseline: the up share of all scored bars of the same series

metrics.why: Because the hidden labels of the pool still exist, the share of the network's hard guesses that match them can be counted, which shows whether it was teaching itself truths or its own mistakes.
metrics.baseline: the larger of the up share and the down share of the masked bars

metrics.why: In the thresholded form the specification describes, this shows how many unlabelled bars cleared the confidence bar and entered training; in Lee's original every drawn pool bar is used, so the share is one by construction.
The training curve changes meaning as the pseudo-label weight ramps in, so it is read only to see that the fit settled and to spot the moment the self-taught term begins to dominate the step.

notApplicable.name: Directional Edge
notApplicable.why: A hit rate above the majority class depends on cutting the probability at one half, which is the engine's rule and not part of the method, so it is reported in the as-run layer only.

notApplicable.name: Gaussian NLL Loss
notApplicable.why: The network outputs a class probability and no Gaussian density of the move, so a Gaussian likelihood never applied to it.

notApplicable.name: Volatility-Adjusted RMSE
notApplicable.why: There is no forecast of the size of the move in this method, because a regressor that pseudo-labels itself gets no gradient.

notApplicable.name: Gaussian negative log-likelihood
notApplicable.why: The network states a probability for a class and never a bell curve over the size of the move, so there is no density to score.

notApplicable.name: Volatility-adjusted root mean square error
notApplicable.why: Pseudo-labeling is defined for classes; a regressor that takes its own output as its target receives no gradient, so there is no price forecast to measure.

notApplicable.name: Sharpe ratio
notApplicable.why: Natively the method outputs a class probability and takes no position, so a risk-adjusted return belongs to the trading rule of the engine and is listed only in the as-run layer.

asRun.standInNote: The runnable model is Lee's original pseudo-labeling in one small fully connected network that reads a single standardised feature row per bar: every unlabelled row drawn into a step gets the network's own hard prediction as its target, with no confidence threshold and no growing labelled set as the specification describes, and the weight of that term rises linearly from the ramp start epoch. The unlabelled pool is manufactured by masking the labels of embargoed blocks of the training span, which deliberately handicaps the model against full supervision, so the as-run numbers measure that network after training on the kept labels plus its own guesses on the masked bars.
asRun.probabilityNote: The probability of up is the sigmoid of the single logit of the kept network read from the bar's standardised feature row alone, with dropout switched off and no calibration curve fitted afterwards.

meaningful.why: The supervised term is unweighted cross-entropy on the kept labels, so the network's output tracks the series' own up share and this score on test bars, which played no part in choosing the kept epoch, is the honest grade of the odds it states.

The network's logit is continuous, so this tests whether a network that spent its later epochs agreeing with its own hard guesses still ranks up bars above down bars, whatever that did to the level of its odds.
A bounded score of the network's probability on every scored bar, read beside the logarithmic loss because the self-confirming term can leave a few very confident misses.

The pseudo-label term rewards the network for moving its logit further toward whichever side it already leaned on the masked bars, and the slope shows whether that left the odds more extreme than the outcomes support.

The fit is not class-weighted, so comparing the network's stated odds with the observed up share in each bin is a fair test; it is read with the count of occupied bins because the odds cluster near one half.
Shows how far the network's odds spread away from their average; a spread that widens without a better logarithmic loss is the signature of the network confirming its own guesses.

The hit rate of calling up when the network's probability is at least one half; with an unweighted fit that cut sits against the kept labels' own up share, so it is read beside the majority-class accuracy.
Averages the hit rate on up bars and on down bars, which shows whether the network learned both sides or whether its hard guesses on the masked bars reinforced a lean toward the commoner class.
One symmetric number for the network's hard call over all four outcome cells, which stays near zero when self-labelling collapsed the call to one side even if the hit rate looks respectable.
What the sign of the network's call earned after costs when every call is traded under the engine's rule; only the side of one half the probability falls on reaches this number.
The steadiness of the per-bar dollars from trading the network's call, costs included; it tests the direction call and the engine's holding rule together and never the size of the probability.
The deepest fall of the equity from trading the network's call, which shows the cost of the stretches where a network taught partly by its own guesses held the wrong side.
Winning dollars over losing dollars of the closed trades that flips of the network's call produced, after costs; it reflects the direction call under the engine's exit rule.
The share of closed trades from the network's call that ended above zero after costs; a trade here is a stretch between flips of the call, not a single prediction.
Shows whether the network called both directions or whether its hard self-labels drove it to one side, and is read beside every trading number of this model together with the count of closed trades.

The accuracy of calling every scored bar the class that was commoner in the fold's training labels, which is the bar that the network's hit rate must clear before its training on masked bars and its own guesses can be said to have taught it anything.

The network's hit rate minus the hit rate of always calling the commoner training class, so a network that only learned the lean of its kept labels, or that confirmed its own lean on the masked bars, shows a lift of about zero.

Counts the closed trades that flips of the network's call produced; a call that rarely flips gives few trades and a net profit resting on a handful of stretches, and a call that flips on every small change of the logit pays costs on each flip.

What holding one position through the same test bars earned after one round trip per fold, which is the only same-series money reference for this network's trading call, because a random-direction trader would pay costs too.
The net profit of trading the network's call minus the buy-and-hold profit of the same folds, which separates a call that added something from one that rode the drift of the series.

The training curve holds the cross-entropy on kept labels plus the ramped cross-entropy against the network's own hard guesses, so it shows that the fit settled and where the self-taught term switched on, and nothing about skill.

measuredNotMeaningful.why: Not computed for this model: the registry gives it no price model, because a regressor that pseudo-labels itself receives no gradient.
Not computed for this model: there is no price model, so no forecast of the move exists whose miss could be measured.
Not computed for this model: there is no price model, so there is no forecast sign to compare with the move.

The training curve holds cross-entropy on kept labels plus the ramped self-agreement term, measured with dropout on, while the validation curve holds only the logarithmic loss of the probability, so their difference compares two different quantities.
With long-only off and no stop or target set the engine is never flat once it has traded, so the share of bars in a position describes the engine's rule and not this network.

caveats: The unlabelled pool is manufactured by masking the labels of embargoed blocks of a fully labelled training span, so every number here is the network with part of its labels deliberately hidden and not a network that had no more labels to use.

The adapter applies no confidence threshold: every pool row drawn into a step is given the network's hard prediction, so the share of the pool admitted is one by construction and the specification's threshold dial does not exist in the run.
The kept epoch is the one with the lowest validation logarithmic loss, so the validation loss curve is optimistic at that epoch and only the test walk is out of sample.

The weight of the pseudo-label term is exactly zero until the ramp start epoch and the epoch with the lowest validation logarithmic loss is restored at the end, so when the kept epoch falls before the ramp start epoch the numbers describe a network trained on the kept labels alone, which never acted on its own guesses; the best epoch in the fit summary read against the ramp start epoch among the fold's recorded parameters shows which happened, and the engine does not flag it.
The engine does not record how many of the network's hard guesses on the masked bars matched the hidden labels, so whether it taught itself truths or mistakes cannot be read from a run today.
The comparison with the same network trained with the pseudo-label weight at zero, which is the test of whether the masked bars helped, is not run by the engine.

The hyperparameter search inside each fold scores trials by the per-bar Sharpe ratio of the real simulator on the training span, not by this network's own loss, and its best score is optimistic by construction.

Consecutive scored bars share future bars because the label looks several bars ahead, so any interval around these numbers needs a block bootstrap or a Newey-West variance and never a binomial interval.
The last bar of every fold exits at its own close while every other exit fills at the next bar's open.
On roots other than the Micro Nasdaq contract the cost per side is that contract's account figure applied as a stated assumption.

consistency_regularization.summary: Predictions must agree under input noise and dropout, against a second pass (Pi-model) or an averaged teacher network (Mean Teacher).
consistency_regularization.implementationNote: Bridge: P(up) from the Mean Teacher's averaged network (or the Pi-model's own); the consistency is the squared gap between two noisy predictions on every span bar. Differs from the spec: Labels are masked in embargoed blocks so there is an unlabelled pool. That deliberately handicaps the model against full supervision. Augmentation is Gaussian noise plus dropout, not time warping. Expect: a smoother, slightly better calibrated plain network.

native.produces: A probability for each class of an input, from a network trained on a few labelled inputs plus many unlabelled ones on which two noisy passes (or a student and its weight-averaged teacher) must give the same answer.
native.targetVariable: the class of each input window (in the specification a market regime or trend label), stated as a probability per class
native.objectiveNote: The unlabelled term is the squared gap between two predictions for the same input under different noise or dropout, taken against a second pass of the same network in the Pi-model or against a teacher whose weights are a running average of the student's in the Mean Teacher, with its weight ramped up from zero.

metrics.why: The labelled term is cross-entropy and the consistency term only asks two noisy passes to agree, so what comes out is still a class probability and it is graded by how much probability it gave to what happened on held-out labelled inputs.
metrics.baseline: quoting the labelled training inputs' class shares for every held-out input

metrics.why: The method's whole claim is that making the student agree with a second noisy pass or with its averaged teacher on unlabelled inputs beats ignoring them, so the same network is trained with the consistency weight at zero and the two scores are compared.
metrics.baseline: the same network, labelled inputs, noise and dropout with the consistency weight set to zero

metrics.why: The specification names this ranking score for its labelled test set; it shows whether the teacher's smoothed probabilities still order the classes correctly, whatever the ramped consistency weight did to their scale.
metrics.baseline: one half, the value of an ordering unrelated to the class

metrics.why: The specification's own evaluation is the hit rate of the most probable class on labelled test inputs; it is read per class and averaged, because a teacher smoothed toward the majority class can score well on the plain hit rate while never recognising the other class.
metrics.baseline: one half, which calling a single class for every input scores

metrics.why: The consistency term is itself a squared gap between two probabilities, so a squared-error score of the final probability against the outcome grades the output on the same scale the regulariser worked on.
metrics.baseline: the same score for always quoting the labelled training inputs' class share

metrics.why: Agreement under noise can be bought by flattening every prediction toward the middle, and weight averaging in the teacher damps extremes further, so the slope shows whether the stated odds ended up too timid or too bold.
metrics.baseline: one, the slope of stated odds that are neither stretched nor squeezed

metrics.why: The cheapest way to make two noisy passes agree is to answer the same thing for every input, so the spread of the probabilities shows whether the consistency weight collapsed the network into a constant.
metrics.baseline: zero spread, which a network that answers identically for every input would show

notApplicable.name: Gaussian NLL Loss
notApplicable.why: The network outputs class probabilities trained by cross-entropy plus a squared consistency gap; it never states a mean and a variance for a return, so a Gaussian likelihood has nothing to score.

notApplicable.name: Volatility-Adjusted RMSE
notApplicable.why: Natively the method is a classifier and forecasts no return size; a price error exists only for the second network the Model Cycle fits beside it.

notApplicable.name: Top-Decile Directional Edge
notApplicable.why: The registry holds no hit rate restricted to the most confident tenth, and the specification never evaluates one; whether confident calls are right more often is read from the calibration slope and the ranking score.

notApplicable.name: Pseudo-label accuracy per round
notApplicable.why: Neither the Pi-model nor the Mean Teacher ever turns a prediction into a hard label for an unlabelled input; the target is the other pass's soft probability, so there are no pseudo-labels to grade.

notApplicable.name: Kept solution's objective on validation minus on training
notApplicable.why: The training objective includes the ramped consistency term and the validation score does not, so the two are different quantities and their difference is not an overfit measure.

asRun.standInNote: The runnable adapter implements the Mean Teacher (or the Pi-model when consistency_teacher is set to it) as published, on a plain multilayer network reading one standardised feature row per bar, but the unlabelled pool is manufactured by masking labels in embargoed blocks of the training span, which deliberately handicaps the model against full supervision, and the two views differ by Gaussian noise and dropout only, not by time warping or image augmentation; the as-run numbers therefore measure a noise-consistent network trained on a labelled subset.
asRun.probabilityNote: The probability of up is the logistic curve applied to the single output of the kept predictor, which for the Mean Teacher is the network whose weights are a running average of the student's and for the Pi-model is the trained network itself; no calibration map is fitted afterwards.

stepQuantity.unit: nats for the validation line; the training line adds the ramped squared consistency gap, in squared probability units times its weight, to the labelled cross-entropy in nats

meaningful.why: The labelled term is unweighted cross-entropy, so the averaged teacher's probability is meant to track the real up share and is graded on test bars by how much probability it gave to what happened; the reference is quoting the fold's training up share.
It asks whether the averaged teacher ranks bars that went up above bars that went down, which holds or fails regardless of how much the consistency term squeezed the probabilities toward the middle.

The consistency term trained on squared gaps between two noisy probabilities, so the squared gap between the teacher's probability and the outcome grades the output on that same scale and stays bounded.

Agreement under noise and weight averaging both damp extreme answers, and the checkpoint was picked on a short validation span, so the slope shows whether the teacher's log-odds came out too timid or too bold.

Because the cross-entropy is not class-weighted the teacher's probability should match the observed up share bin by bin; a teacher that barely leaves the middle fills only the central bins, so the occupied-bin count is read with it.

Two noisy passes agree most easily when the answer is the same for every bar, so the spread of the teacher's probability shows whether the ramped consistency weight flattened the network into a constant.

The share of test bars where the side of one half the teacher's probability fell on matched the direction, read against the majority-class accuracy of the same fold; the cut sits on an unweighted probability, so it leans toward the labelled up share.

A teacher smoothed toward the labelled up share can call almost every bar the majority way and still score well on plain accuracy, so the hit rate averaged over up bars and down bars shows whether it recognises both.
One symmetric number over all four confusion cells for the teacher's hard calls, which drops to zero when consistency smoothing leaves it calling a single direction.

It is what going long when the teacher's probability is at least one half and short otherwise earned after costs under the engine's rule of following the latest call; only the side of one half reaches this number.
It sets the teacher's trading result against simply holding the contract over the same folds, which matters because a smoothed network that mostly says up looks profitable on a rising tape.

Per-bar net result of the teacher's calls over its own variability; zero is an arithmetic marker and not a no-skill line, because a teacher hovering around one half flips often and pays costs each time.
The deepest fall of the equity built from the teacher's calls; it describes the path the engine's trading rule produced and nothing the consistency objective trained for.

Winners over losers among the trades created when the teacher's probability crosses one half; one is an arithmetic marker, and it is read with the trade count because a smoothed probability may cross rarely.
The share of those trades that closed above zero after costs; it says how often a crossing of one half by the teacher paid, not how large the wins and losses were.

The forecast comes from a second network of the same method trained with a Huber loss on the scaled move, with the consistency term taken as the squared gap between two noisy value predictions; skill against the no-change forecast tests that second network, not the direction teacher.

The second network's miss in points after its output is multiplied back by the trailing move scale and rounded to the tick; a noise-consistent value network stays near zero, so it is read beside the no-change error.

Whether the sign of the second network's forecast matched the actual move on bars where both are non-zero after tick rounding; it can disagree with the traded call, which comes from the direction teacher.

measuredNotMeaningful.why: The training line is labelled cross-entropy plus the ramped consistency gap measured on the student, while the validation line is the plain logarithmic loss of the kept predictor, so their difference is not an overfit measure.
When the run is not long-only and no stop or target is set the engine is always in the market once the first call is made, so exposure describes the engine's rule and not the teacher.

caveats: The unlabelled pool is manufactured by masking: labels are hidden in blocks of label_block_bars with an embargo of the label horizon, and only the labeled_fraction that remains feeds the cross-entropy, which deliberately handicaps the model against full supervision.
The consistency term draws from every bar of the training span, labelled bars included, so it regularises the labelled rows as well as the hidden ones.
The epoch kept is the one with the lowest validation logarithmic loss, so the validation loss shown for it is optimistic; only the test walk is out of sample.
The price forecast belongs to a second network fitted separately with a Huber loss and is not the network that makes the direction call.

Consecutive scored bars share future bars because the label looks several bars ahead, so any interval around these numbers needs a block bootstrap or a Newey-West variance and never a binomial interval.
For roots other than MNQ the costs charged are the MNQ account figures, a stated assumption, and the last bar of each fold exits at its close while every other exit fills at the next open.

fixmatch.summary: A confident prediction on a lightly perturbed unlabelled bar becomes the target for a heavily perturbed copy of it (Sohn et al. 2020).
fixmatch.implementationNote: Bridge: P(up) from one network; a confident weak-view prediction is the hard target of a strong view (noise, masked features, scaled row). Differs from the spec: Labels are masked in embargoed blocks so there is an unlabelled pool. That deliberately handicaps the model against full supervision. Tabular noise replaces RandAugment; the price model keeps low-spread Monte-Carlo dropout guesses. Expect: few bars pass the threshold.

native.produces: A class probability for each real input from a discriminator that is trained at the same time to tell real inputs from the inputs a generator makes out of random noise, together with those generated inputs as a by-product.
native.targetVariable: The class of the trading signal attached to a real input window (buy, sell or hold), stated as a probability per class, learned from a small labelled set, a large unlabelled set and the generator's forgeries.
native.objectiveNote: The unlabelled-data term is the discriminator's adversarial loss for calling unlabelled inputs real and generated inputs fake, added to the cross-entropy of its class output on labelled inputs, while the generator is trained against it; the adversarial game itself is not the score, and as run the unlabelled pool is manufactured by masking the labels of embargoed blocks of a fully labelled series.

metrics.why: The discriminator's class output is trained by cross-entropy on the labelled inputs, so the first question is how much probability that class output gave to what actually followed on inputs outside the training set.
metrics.baseline: The logarithmic loss of quoting the training set's class shares on every scored input.

metrics.why: The claim is that learning to reject the generator's forgeries teaches the discriminator features that help it classify, so its score is compared with the same discriminator trained on the labelled inputs alone with no generator and no real-or-fake term.
metrics.baseline: The same discriminator body and class output on the same folds with the adversarial term and the generator switched off.

metrics.why: The specification names this ranking measure for its own evaluation, and it shows whether the class output sorts real inputs correctly even after an unstable adversarial game has pushed the level of its probabilities around.
metrics.baseline: One half, the value of an output that carries no ordering information.

metrics.why: The real-or-fake term rewards the discriminator for large class logits on every real input, labelled or not, which can stretch the class odds beyond what the outcomes support, and the slope measures that stretch.
metrics.baseline: One, the slope of a probability whose scale is right.

metrics.why: A bounded squared-error score of the class output that stays readable in the epochs where the adversarial game makes the discriminator briefly and wildly over-confident.
metrics.baseline: The Brier score of quoting the training set's class shares on every scored input.

metrics.why: The generator's forged inputs are a by-product, and the share of real inputs that lie inside the neighbourhood of the forgeries only describes how widely the forgeries spread over the real inputs; it is shown with no better or worse direction, because the specification's own Bad GAN variant improves the classifier with forgeries that deliberately do not cover the real inputs.

The discriminator's supervised term, its real-or-fake term and the generator's loss plotted as separate curves show only whether the game stayed balanced or one side won; none of the three is a score of the classifier.

notApplicable.name: Wasserstein Distance
notApplicable.why: The discriminator is trained with a logarithmic real-or-fake loss, not as a constrained critic, so it never estimates a transport distance.

notApplicable.name: Reconstruction MSE
notApplicable.why: There is no encoder and decoder pair in this model, so no input is ever rebuilt and no reconstruction error exists.

notApplicable.name: Fréchet Market Distance
notApplicable.why: The registry has no such metric, and sample realism is not what this model is judged on because its product is the discriminator's class output.

notApplicable.name: Latent KL Divergence
notApplicable.why: The model has no encoder posterior and no prior-matching term; that row belongs to a variational autoencoder and was stamped here by mistake.

notApplicable.name: Latent Uniformity
notApplicable.why: The model learns no normalised embedding whose spread over a sphere could be measured; that row belongs to contrastive representation learning.

notApplicable.name: Wasserstein distance
notApplicable.why: The discriminator described is trained with a logarithmic real-or-fake loss and is not a critic constrained to estimate a transport distance, so it yields no Wasserstein distance.

notApplicable.name: Reconstruction mean squared error
notApplicable.why: The model has a generator and a discriminator but no encoder that maps a real input to a code and back, so nothing is ever reconstructed.

notApplicable.name: Fréchet market distance
notApplicable.why: It grades how lifelike the generator's samples are, but the product of this model is the discriminator's class output, and a semi-supervised discriminator can classify well beside a generator whose samples are poor.

notApplicable.name: Latent Kullback-Leibler divergence
notApplicable.why: The generator draws its noise straight from a fixed distribution and there is no encoder posterior to compare with a prior, so no divergence term exists in this model.

notApplicable.name: Latent uniformity
notApplicable.why: The model learns no embedding on a sphere whose spread could be measured; the generator's noise is uniform or Gaussian by construction.

notApplicable.name: Classifier two-sample test accuracy of generated inputs
notApplicable.why: For the semi-supervised adversarial network the classifier is the product, so a test of whether a fresh judge can tell forged inputs from real ones grades the by-product and not the result.

notApplicable.name: Held-out log-likelihood per row
notApplicable.why: A generator fed by noise defines samples but no density and no bound on one, so there is no likelihood of unseen inputs to report.

asRun.standInNote: The runnable model is the feature-matching form of Salimans and colleagues: one discriminator with two class logits and the generated class left implicit, and a generator trained to match the discriminator's average hidden features, where the specification's main text describes a separate real-or-fake head and a generator trained to fool it. Both networks work on one standardised feature row per bar, not on price windows, and no price model exists. The unlabelled pool is manufactured by masking the labels of embargoed blocks of the training span, which deliberately handicaps the model against full supervision, so the as-run numbers measure the discriminator's two class logits after that training.
asRun.probabilityNote: The probability of up is the softmax over the discriminator's two class logits, computed as the sigmoid of the up logit minus the down logit, with the implicit generated class left out, the input noise switched off at prediction time and no calibration curve fitted afterwards.

meaningful.why: The discriminator's supervised term is unweighted cross-entropy over its two class logits on the kept labels, so its output tracks the series' own up share and this score on test bars, which played no part in choosing the kept epoch, is the honest grade of its odds.

The gap between the two class logits is continuous, so this tests whether a discriminator that also learned to reject the generator's rows ranks up bars above down bars, however the adversarial term moved the level of its odds.
A bounded score of the discriminator's class probability on every scored bar, which stays readable when the real-or-fake term has inflated both class logits and produced a few very confident misses.

The real-or-fake term rewards a large combined size of the two class logits on every real bar, which can widen the gap between them, and the slope shows whether the resulting odds are more extreme than the outcomes support.

The fit is not class-weighted, so comparing the discriminator's stated odds with the observed up share in each bin is a fair test; it is read with the count of occupied bins because the odds cluster near one half.
An adversarial game that the generator loses early leaves the discriminator rejecting forgeries easily and learning little about direction, and a small spread of its class probability reveals that.
The hit rate of calling up when the up logit is at least the down logit; with an unweighted fit that cut sits at the labelled bars' own up share, so it is read beside the majority-class accuracy.
Averages the hit rate on up bars and on down bars, which shows whether the discriminator's class logits learned both sides or leaned toward whichever class was commoner among the kept labels.
One symmetric number for the discriminator's hard class call over all four outcome cells, which stays near zero when the call is one-sided even if the hit rate looks respectable.
What the sign of the gap between the discriminator's class logits earned after costs when every call is traded under the engine's rule; the size of the gap never reaches this number.

The steadiness of the per-bar dollars from trading the discriminator's class call, costs included; it tests the direction call and the engine's holding rule together and never the size of the probability.
The deepest fall of the equity produced by trading the discriminator's class call, which shows the cost of the stretches where an unstable adversarial fit held the wrong side.
Winning dollars over losing dollars of the closed trades that flips of the discriminator's class call produced, after costs; it reflects the direction call under the engine's exit rule.
The share of closed trades from the discriminator's class call that ended above zero after costs; a trade here is a stretch between flips of the call, not a single prediction.
Shows whether the discriminator called both directions or collapsed to one side, and is read beside every trading number of this model together with the count of closed trades.

The training curve holds the discriminator's cross-entropy plus its weighted real-or-fake term and leaves out the generator's feature-matching loss, so it shows the balance of the game from one side and is not a score of the classifier.

measuredNotMeaningful.why: Not computed: this model has no price model, because its generator makes feature rows and nothing in it forecasts the size of the move.
Not computed: this model has no price model, so there is no forecast in points whose miss could be measured.
Not computed: this model has no price model, so there is no forecast sign to compare with the move; direction comes only from the discriminator's class logits.
The training curve holds cross-entropy plus the weighted real-or-fake term while the validation curve holds the class logarithmic loss alone, so their difference compares two different quantities.
With long-only off and no stop or target set the engine is never flat once it has traded, so the share of bars in a position describes the engine's rule and not this model.

caveats: The unlabelled pool is manufactured by masking the labels of embargoed blocks of a fully labelled training span, so every number here is the model with part of its labels deliberately hidden and not a model that had no more labels to use.

The kept epoch is the one with the lowest validation logarithmic loss of the class output, not a point where the adversarial game settled, so the generator at that epoch may be poor and the validation loss curve is optimistic there.
The generated rows are standardised feature rows that are never scored or stored, so nothing in a run says how widely the generator's rows spread over the real bars.
The comparison with the same discriminator trained on the kept labels alone, which is the test of whether the adversarial term helped, is not run by the engine.
Adversarial training is unstable, so two runs that differ only in seed can give visibly different results and one run is weak evidence.

The hyperparameter search inside each fold scores trials by the per-bar Sharpe ratio of the real simulator on the training span, not by this model's own loss, and its best score is optimistic by construction.

Consecutive scored bars share future bars because the label looks several bars ahead, so any interval around these numbers needs a block bootstrap or a Newey-West variance and never a binomial interval.
The last bar of every fold exits at its own close while every other exit fills at the next bar's open.
On roots other than the Micro Nasdaq contract the cost per side is that contract's account figure applied as a stated assumption.
